def ridge(Xtr,ytr,alpha,w=None):
    mu=Xtr.mean(0); sd=Xtr.std(0)+1e-9

def cv(cols, alpha=10, train_dec_only=False, wdec=1.0, verbose=False):

`submission.py` is final. It is a time-only forecaster, and it scores person-balanced MAE 0.286 on development, against 0.539 for the template baseline. The one development person it misses badly is H17, with MAE 0.756.

**What the predictor does**
- `predict(request)` is stateless and uses only the standard library (`math`).
- It computes elapsed minutes `e = history[-1].time_min − history[0].time_min`, so absolute and shifted clocks don't matter. The only causal input it uses is the `time_min` column.
- The mean is a ridge-regularised least-absolute-deviation fit (so MAE-optimal) on `e` and `log(e+1)`, with the inputs clipped to the training range.
- It was fit on all 14 training people, using every origin with `e` from 2 to 44. The target is `core(t+15)`. Rows with a missing core value (H09's last rows) are skipped.
- The mean is clipped to 35–41 °C. The interval is the mean ±0.7 °C, so the width is a constant 1.4 °C, inside the 0–5 °C limit.
- A 3B or horizon-0 request uses a second fit of the same form on the current core temperature. That fit is untested on development.
- No heart rate, skin temperature, watts, anthropometric, ambient or humidity inputs are used.

**Evidence from the runs**

| Model | Dev person-balanced MAE | H17 MAE | Leave-one-person-out MAE on training origins after the first watts decrease |
|---|---|---|---|
| Template baseline | 0.539 | — | ~0.45 |
| 7 features (adds mass, age, W/kg, skin) | 0.510 | 1.226 | 0.15–0.17 |
| Same without age | 0.331 | 0.990 | 0.24–0.27 |
| Time-only (final) | 0.286 | 0.756 | ~0.235–0.255 |

- The 7-feature model looked much better in leave-one-person-out CV, but that CV was also used to choose the features, and the gain came mostly from age. It did not hold up on the four development people, so I dropped it.
- None of the single features I tried, each added to the time-only model, reliably beat it in CV. Tree models were no better either.
- The final model's development MAE per person is H08 0.086, H17 0.756, H20 0.108 and H24 0.193. The hot-subset MAE is 0.061.
- H17 appears to run roughly 0.8–1.0 °C cooler than any model predicted. I could not find a feature that flags such a person.

**Uncertainty**
- I chose the ±0.7 °C half-width by balancing the training CV against development. Leave-one-person-out residuals favoured about ±0.5 °C.
- I settled on ±0.7 °C after dev interval score fell from 3.18 (±0.3) to 3.02 (±0.5), 2.75 (±0.6) and 2.47 (±0.7).
- Development coverage is 0.76, well below the 90% target. The H17 errors are mostly larger than the interval, and widening further costs width everywhere else.
- Each person's starting core temperature, and so their overall level, is unobserved. Roughly 0.2–0.3 °C of person-level error can't be removed with these inputs. Errors also grow later in a session.

**Limitations**
- Hidden test people with unusual physiology, like H17, will be missed. The model also ignores any information the heart rate, skin or watts data might carry.
- It assumes the history starts at the beginning of the session.
- Only 14 training people and 4 development people were available, so all the estimates above are noisy.
- Development was queried seven times. I used it only to compare model families and interval widths, not to fit parameters.
